pos: n. (Theodore Tronchin, 1582–1657, professor at Geneva and delegate to the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Greek Theodoros, gift of God; French Tronchin, a Geneva family name of Provencal origin.
biblical_def: Theodore Tronchin held a Geneva chair for nearly fifty years and was the city's delegate to the Synod of Dort. He had studied Hebrew under the best masters of his generation, taught it before he taught theology, and spent decades building up the library and the manuscript collection of the Academy. At Dort he stood with the majority for the Canons as adopted. At home he kept Geneva orthodox through the years when the French Reformed academies were beginning to soften, and he held the line in print against Rome. He belongs in the dictionary as the second generation's characteristic figure: not a founder, but the man who kept what the founders left, which Scripture treats as an office in its own right (1Ti 6:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines trust as that which is committed to one's care, and landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land.
webster_full: TRUST, n. That which is committed to one's care; charge received in confidence.
LAND'MARK, n. A mark to designate the boundary of land; any mark or fixed object by which the limits of a farm or estate may be known.
DEPOS'IT, n. That which is lodged in the hands of a person for safe keeping.
ACAD'EMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university or college and a common school.
scriptures: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Fifty years in a Geneva chair, keeping what Calvin and Beza had left.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern preference for the founder over the keeper, which treats conservation as a lesser calling than innovation. Scripture does not rank them that way. Timothy is given a deposit and told to keep it, and the warning attached names the thing most likely to take it from him: oppositions of science falsely so called, that is, the learned fashion of the hour.

The principle to recover is that the boundary was set by somebody else and is not the present generation's to move. “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). The deposit is a thing handed over and handed on: “O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings” (1Ti 6:20). And the faith itself was given once: “the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).

pos: n. (Benedetto Turrettini, 1588–1631, professor and pastor at Geneva)
etymology: Latin benedictus, blessed, well spoken of; Italian Turrettini, from torre, a tower.
biblical_def: Benedict Turretin was the first of his family to serve Geneva and the father of the Francis Turretin whose systematic theology became the standard of Reformed orthodoxy. The Turrettini were Lucchese: Protestant merchants driven out of Italy by the Inquisition, who settled in Geneva and gave it three generations of ministers. Benedict taught theology, preached, travelled to the Netherlands to raise money for Geneva's fortifications when the city expected a siege, and defended the Geneva Bible against the Roman charge that the Reformed had corrupted the text. He died at forty-three. The dictionary notes him partly for himself and partly because the line of three Turrettini is a plain lesson in how God provides for a church: he gives it a family (Psa 48:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines generation as a single succession of men in descent, and bulwark as a fortification or means of defence.
webster_full: GENERA'TION, n. A single succession of natural descent, as the children of the same parents; the people of the same period.
BUL'WARK, n. A bastion, or a rampart; a mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting cannon shot; a fortification.
EX'ILE, n. The state of being expelled from one's native country; banishment.
SUCCES'SION, n. A following of things in order; a series of things following one another in time or place.

Deu 4:9

Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes have seen, and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life: but teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons;
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: A Lucchese exile family that gave Geneva three generations of ministers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suspicion of inherited calling, which reads a son in his father's office as nepotism and nothing else. The abuse is real, and Scripture records plenty of it among the priests of Israel; but the pattern itself is a covenant pattern. God deals with households and not only with individuals, and the Turrettini are an ordinary instance of an extraordinary promise.

The principle to recover is that the covenant runs to the seed, and that a father's teaching is the appointed means. “And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant” (Gen 17:7). The psalmist makes the purpose of a city's defences a lesson for the children: “Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following” (Psa 48:13).

pos: n. (Antoine Leger, 1596–1661, Geneva pastor, chaplain at Constantinople, professor of theology)
etymology: Latin Antonius, a Roman family name; French Leger, from Latin Leodegarius.
biblical_def: Antoine Leger was a Waldensian of the Piedmont valleys who served as chaplain to the Dutch embassy at Constantinople for over a decade and then as professor of theology at Geneva. At Constantinople he was close to Cyril Lucaris, the patriarch who tried to bring the Greek church toward Reformed doctrine, and he had a hand in the project to put the New Testament into the spoken Greek of the day so that ordinary Greeks could read it. Lucaris was strangled by the Turks in 1638 and the attempt collapsed. Leger went home, taught, and kept up the cause of his own Waldensian people under persecution. Philip's question to the Ethiopian is the whole case for a translation into the language men actually speak: understandest thou what thou readest? (Act 8:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines version as a translation, and vernacular as native, belonging to the country of one's birth.
webster_full: VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
CHAP'LAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the care of a chapel; a clergyman who belongs to a ship of war, or to a regiment, or to an embassy.
PA'TRIARCH, n. A dignitary superior to the order of archbishops; as the patriarch of Constantinople.

And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?

How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: A Waldensian at Constantinople, trying to put the New Testament into spoken Greek.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the clerical instinct that keeps the text in a language the people cannot read, whether the language is Latin, liturgical Greek, or the private dialect of a teaching class. The Greek church of the seventeenth century read the New Testament in a Greek most Greeks no longer spoke, and Lucaris and Leger were answering that. Rome had made the same error with the Vulgate and the Reformation was in large part the undoing of it.

The principle to recover is that the word is to be understood, and that a guide is given for that purpose and no other. “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30). The eunuch's answer states the need plainly: “How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Act 8:31). And Paul runs the chain back to its first link: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14).

pos: n. (Nicolas Colladon, c. 1530–1586, Geneva pastor and first biographer of Calvin)
etymology: Greek Nikolaos, victor of the people; French Colladon, a Berry family name.
biblical_def: Nicolas Colladon was one of the Frenchmen who came to Geneva for the gospel and stayed to serve it. He was a pastor and professor there, rector of the Academy, and he wrote the fuller of the two early lives of Calvin, a year-by-year account drawn from the registers and from his own memory of the man. He fell out with the magistrates over the Company of Pastors' independence, left for Lausanne, and taught there until he died. His biography is the reason later generations know what Calvin's working weeks were actually like, and the dictionary values it for the same reason it values any faithful record: a life rightly told is a form of instruction (Heb 13:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines biography as the history of the life and character of a particular person, and register as a written account.
webster_full: BIOG'RAPHY, n. The history of the life and character of a particular person.
REG'ISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings, for preserving and conveying the knowledge of them.
REC'TOR, n. The chief elective officer of some universities; also, a clergyman who has the charge of a parish.
MEM'OIR, n. A written account; memorial account; a history composed from personal experience and memory.

Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: The fuller early life of Calvin, written from the registers by a man who was there.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the hagiography that smooths a man into an emblem, and its mirror image, the modern biography that exists to find the feet of clay. Colladon does neither. He gives the years, the sermons, the illnesses, the controversies and the quantity of work, and the reader is left to make the judgment that Hebrews asks for.

The principle to recover is that the lives of faithful men are given to the church for imitation, and that the imitation is of their faith and not of their circumstances. “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7). The witnesses are a cloud, not a monument: “let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1).

pos: n. (Charles Perrot, 1541–1608, Geneva pastor and professor)
etymology: Germanic Karl, a man, a freeman, through French Charles; French Perrot, a diminutive of Pierre.
biblical_def: Charles Perrot served Geneva for forty years, first as the country pastor at Genthod and Moens outside the walls, then in the city and in the Academy, and he was among the men who carried the Company of Pastors after Beza grew old. He is remembered for a particular moderation: a conviction that the Reformed churches should not break communion over matters the Scriptures had not settled, together with a complete refusal to treat the gospel itself as unsettled. That is a difficult position to hold and easy to caricature from either side. The dictionary records it as the right instinct, with the boundary stated in Paul's own terms, because a church that cannot distinguish the faith from its own customs will either divide over nothing or surrender everything (1Th 5:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines moderation as a restraint of violent passions or indulgences, and essential as necessary to the existence of a thing.
webster_full: MODERA'TION, n. Restraint of violent passions or indulgence of appetite; calmness of mind; equanimity.
ESSEN'TIAL, a. Necessary to the existence of a thing; as, extension and figure are essential properties of bodies.
IN'DIFFERENT, a. Neutral; not inclined to either side; impartial.
COM'MUNION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; interchange of transactions.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Rom 14:8
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.
corruption_summary: Forty years at Geneva, holding that not everything is essential and the gospel is.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the collapse of this distinction in both directions. One party makes everything essential and divides over the furniture; the other makes nothing essential and has no gospel to divide over. Perrot's position survives only where a church knows which articles it would die for, and the seventeenth century shows how quickly a moderation without that knowledge becomes indifference.

The principle to recover is that proving and holding fast belong together. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21). The boundary is absolute and admits no moderation at all: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). Within the boundary the blessing is real: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1).

pos: n. (Simon Goulart, 1543–1628, Geneva pastor, editor and translator)
etymology: Hebrew Shimon, hearing, through Greek Simon; French Goulart, a Senlis family name.
biblical_def: Simon Goulart pastored in Geneva for more than fifty years and produced an output that is hard to credit: translations from Latin and Greek, editions of the Fathers and of the Reformers, commentaries, histories of the French wars, collections of martyr accounts, and the moderating of the Company of Pastors after Beza died. He wrote and edited because the presses of Geneva were the arsenal of the French Reformed churches, and a church under persecution needs books more than it needs committees. Not much of it is read now, and almost none of it was original; that was the point. A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver (Pro 25:11), and Goulart spent a long life setting other men's words in silver so that the French churches could have them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines editor as one who prepares a work for publication, and translate as to interpret in another language.
webster_full: ED'ITOR, n. A publisher; particularly, a person who superintends an impression of a book; one who revises and prepares a work for publication.
TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
PRESS, n. A machine for printing; called a printing-press.
MAR'TYROLOGY, n. A history or account of martyrs with their sufferings.
scriptures: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
corruption_summary: Fifty years in a Geneva pulpit and an output of translations, editions and histories.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the premium the modern world puts on originality, which leaves the translator, editor and compiler looking like a man who had no ideas of his own. Goulart had plenty and spent them on other men's books, because a persecuted church in France needed Augustine, Calvin and the martyr accounts in print and in French more than it needed his opinions.

The principle to recover is that the written record is for the use of those who come after, and comfort is one of its stated purposes. “For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope” (Rom 15:4). The craftsman's own standard is Solomon's: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11).

pos: n. (Gaspard Laurent, 1556–1636, pastor and rector of the Academy of Geneva)
etymology: Persian Gaspar, treasurer, through French Gaspard; Latin Laurentius, from laurus, the laurel.
biblical_def: Gaspard Laurent was a Geneva pastor and professor who served as rector of the Academy and spent his long life in the ordinary offices of that church: preaching, teaching the arts and theology, sitting in the Company of Pastors, examining candidates for the ministry. He left little that is read today. He is in the dictionary deliberately, as one instance of the great majority of faithful men: a name in a register, a signature on a set of academic theses, a pulpit filled for decades, and no monument. The Authorized Version is realistic about this. Most of the people of God are not recorded by name anywhere but in the book of life, and the men who taught them are recorded in the same place and nowhere else (1Co 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines faithful as firm in adherence to the truth and to the duties of religion, and obscure as not noted, unknown.
webster_full: FAITH'FUL, a. Firm in adherence to the truth and to the duties of religion; constant in the performance of duties or services.
OBSCURE', a. Not noted; unknown; undistinguished; as a man of obscure birth.
REC'TOR, n. The chief elective officer of some universities; also, a clergyman who has the charge of a parish.
STEW'ARDSHIP, n. The office of a steward; the management of another's concerns.

corruption_summary: Rector of the Academy, eighty years of life, and almost nothing left to read.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that what is not remembered did not matter, which is a historian's convenience mistaken for a judgment. The Academy of Geneva trained the ministers of France, Scotland, Hungary and the Low Countries, and it did so through men like Laurent whose names survive mainly on title pages of theses they presided over.

The principle to recover is that the standard for a servant is faithfulness and not fame, and that the accounting is not done here. “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). The office is defined by what the lips keep, whoever is watching: “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7).

pos: n. (Jean Jaquemot, 1553–1615, Geneva pastor and Latin poet)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through French Jean; Jaquemot, a Lorraine family name.
biblical_def: Jean Jaquemot was a pastor of Geneva who wrote Latin verse. He produced metrical paraphrases of Scripture, sacred poems, and the occasional pieces that the learned culture of the period expected on a death, a marriage or an academic occasion. The dictionary includes him because the Reformed churches have a long and sometimes forgotten literary tradition of exactly this kind, and because the question his work raises is a live one: what is poetry for, in a church governed by the regulative principle? The answer the Reformed gave is clear enough in practice. In corporate worship, the Psalms and what Scripture commands; outside it, the whole range of lawful art, used for instruction and delight. Paraphrase is not inspiration, and the distinction must be kept visible (2Pe 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines paraphrase as an explanation of some text in other and ampler terms, and verse as a line consisting of a certain succession of sounds.
webster_full: PAR'APHRASE, n. An explanation of some text or passage in other and ampler terms than those used by the author.
VERSE, n. A line, consisting of a certain succession of sounds and number of syllables; metrical language.
PO'ETRY, n. The language of excited imagination and feeling, usually in metrical form.
PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
scriptures: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
Exo 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
corruption_summary: Latin verse from a Geneva pulpit, and the line between paraphrase and the text.
corruption_paragraphs: A real danger attends this work and the dictionary names it. A metrical paraphrase that is loved can quietly replace the verse it paraphrases, and whole congregations have ended up singing a poet's theology under the impression that they were singing Scripture. The remedy is not to forbid the art but to keep the labels honest: this is the text, and that is a man's rendering of it.

The principle to recover is that the Scripture is not the private property of its expositor, poet or preacher. “Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20). What is written was written for a purpose outside the writer: “For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning” (Rom 15:4). And the worship that Scripture regulates, it regulates by command: “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8).

pos: n. (Louis Tronchin, 1629–1705, professor of theology at Geneva)
etymology: Germanic Hlodovic, famous warrior, through French Louis; Tronchin, a Geneva family name.
biblical_def: Louis Tronchin was the son of Theodore Tronchin and held a Geneva chair for nearly half a century, and in that time he moved the city away from the position his father had defended. He had studied at Saumur, absorbed the softer account of the atonement taught there, took up the new Cartesian philosophy, and worked steadily against the Helvetic Consensus of 1675, the formula by which the Swiss churches bound their ministers to the strict Reformed doctrine of the covenants and of Scripture. He prevailed in the long run. Within two generations Geneva had loosened its subscription, and within three it had largely abandoned the doctrine of its own Academy. The dictionary records the case because it is the clearest instance of how a Reformed church is lost: not by apostasy in the pulpit but by a chair, a generation, and a formula quietly set aside (Pro 22:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subscription as a signing of one's name in attestation, and declension as a falling off, a decay.
webster_full: SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of underwriting or signing one's name; attestation given by underwriting the name.
DECLEN'SION, n. A falling off; decay; gradual failure or diminution of strength.
FOR'MULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model; a prescribed form of words in which a doctrine is stated.
INNOVA'TION, n. Change made by the introduction of something new; a novelty.
scriptures: Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Heb 13:9
Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats, which have not profited them that have been occupied therein.
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
corruption_summary: The son who unmade his father's work, and Geneva lost its own doctrine in three generations.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named plainly. Louis Tronchin opposed the Helvetic Consensus, favoured the Saumur account of a universal atonement conditionally applied, and welcomed a philosophy that begins with the mind's own doubt. Each move looked moderate and defensible on its own; together they removed the fences, and the Geneva of 1750 bore little resemblance to the Geneva of 1650. The men who loosen a subscription rarely intend the destination, which is precisely why the warning is given in terms of boundaries rather than of intentions.

The principle to recover is that doctrinal fences are inherited property, and the generation that finds them did not build them. “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). The instruction when the way is in question is to look backward, not inward: “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). Paul names the alternative: “tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14).

“Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines” (Heb 13:9) — Saumur's atonement and Descartes's doubt.
“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — and Geneva lost its Academy's doctrine.

pos: n. (Robert Chouet, 1642–1731, professor of philosophy at Geneva and magistrate)
etymology: Germanic Hrodberht, bright in fame, through French Robert; Chouet, a Geneva printing family's name.
biblical_def: Robert Chouet taught philosophy at Saumur and then at Geneva, and he was the man who brought Cartesian natural philosophy into the Genevan Academy in place of the Aristotelian course it had inherited. He later left teaching for the city's government and served as a magistrate for decades. The dictionary treats the change he made with care rather than with alarm. In natural philosophy, the study of bodies, motion and mechanism, the Reformed were free to follow the evidence, and much of what Chouet taught about the physical world was simply better than what it replaced. The danger lay next door, in the method that would make doubt the first principle of all knowledge, including the knowledge of God, and that door was pushed open in the same generation (Pro 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philosophy as the knowledge of the causes which produce the phenomena of nature, and doubt as a fluctuation of mind respecting truth.
webster_full: PHILOS'OPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of the phenomena or effects of nature, and of the causes which produce them.
DOUBT, n. A fluctuation of mind respecting truth or propriety, arising from defect of knowledge or evidence.
MECHAN'ICAL, a. Pertaining to machines, or to the art of constructing machines; according to the laws of mechanism.
MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
scriptures: Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
Job 38:4
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: He put Descartes in the Genevan lecture hall, and the door next to it opened too.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary distinguishes two things the seventeenth century often confused. Cartesian physics, the mechanical account of the natural world, is a question for evidence and the Reformed were never bound to Aristotle. Cartesian method in theology, the proposal that a man begin by doubting everything and build upward from his own certainty of himself, inverts the order of knowing: it makes revelation a witness summoned before the human mind rather than the Word before which the mind is silent. Chouet taught the first; his colleagues in divinity were soon drawing on the second.

The principle to recover is that the creature's understanding is a derived and limited instrument and knows it. “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5). The LORD puts the matter to Job as a question of standing, not of cleverness: “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4). And Paul ends his longest argument in the only posture available: “how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out” (Rom 11:33).
